Q434.L1t: Contracts for the sale of goods between merchants are governed by Article 2 of the UCC, which has its own rules on formation and modification.
Q434.L2t: The contract here was for the sale of bread, so it is a sale of goods under the UCC, and the parties signed a separate sheet saying modifications must be in writing.
Q434.L3t: Under the UCC a good-faith modification needs no new consideration, but a signed agreement that excludes modification except by a signed writing can be modified only by a signed writing, and the May 1 change was agreed only by telephone.
Q434.L4t: The restaurant is not obligated to pay the extra $20, because the oral price increase did not satisfy the contract's written-modification requirement and so is unenforceable under the UCC.
Q434.L2f: The contract was a requirements-and-minimum agreement for bread that the parties signed on December 30 and had performed fully for four months before the dispute.
Q434.L3f: Under the UCC, a no-oral-modification clause is ineffective against a merchant who has already shipped goods in reliance on an oral change, since the shipment makes the modification binding.
Q434.L4f: The restaurant must pay the extra $20, because the bakery relied to its detriment on the oral price increase by making the May shipment, which makes the modification enforceable.

Q441.L1t: Evidence law limits what a party may offer at trial in order to keep out proof that is irrelevant or unfairly prejudicial.
Q441.L2t: The girl's parents are suing the lumber company for negligence over a truck driver's conduct, and the company's liability may turn on whether the driver was its employee.
Q441.L3t: Character evidence, such as a person's general reputation for careless driving, is generally inadmissible in a civil case to prove that the person acted negligently on the particular occasion.
Q441.L4t: The reputation evidence is least likely to be admissible, because a driver's general reputation for poor driving cannot be used to show negligent conduct on this occasion.
Q441.L2f: The truck driver was driving a loaded tractor-trailer owned by the lumber company when the 11-year-old girl ran into the road, and the vehicle struck her despite his braking.
Q441.L3f: A criminal guilty plea is inadmissible in a later civil suit against a different party, because it is hearsay not covered by any exception and is unduly prejudicial.
Q441.L4f: The evidence that the truck driver pleaded guilty to the DUI charge is the least likely to be admitted, because a criminal plea cannot be used in the civil trial.

Q435.L1t: The hearsay rule excludes out-of-court statements offered for their truth unless an exception applies, and several exceptions cover family and personal history.
Q435.L2t: Birth date is a matter of personal or family history, and the hearsay rules include exceptions for records of family history and for public records of births.
Q435.L3t: An affidavit is a sworn out-of-court statement by someone who is not testifying, and the brother's affidavit fits no hearsay exception, whereas the other items fall under family-history or vital-records exceptions.
Q435.L4t: The brother's sworn affidavit is inadmissible, because it is hearsay that fits no exception.
Q435.L2f: The insured's age is usually proved only through a certified copy of a government birth record, and the court will not accept any other family documents on this point.
Q435.L3f: Statements of age engraved on a family portrait are mere unsworn assertions made for no reliable purpose, and they fall within no hearsay exception for family history.
Q435.L4f: The family portrait with ages engraved on it is inadmissible to prove the insured's birth date, because the engraving is hearsay that no exception covers.
